strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1,061,791 training pairs) is roughly 6.7x larger than the previous largest open-source MER dataset (Pix2tex, 158,480), and UniMER-Test provides a multi-dimensional benchmark (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE, 23,789 samples) that exposes clear weaknesses of existing models, e.g., Pix2tex dropping to BLEU 0.092 on SCE and 0.012 on HWE (Table 5, Fig. 1).

Comprehensive evaluation across both printed and handwritten settings: the model is compared against dedicated HMER systems (CAN, SAN, BTTR, CoMER) on CROHME 2014/2016/2019 and HME100K, and reports state-of-the-art ExpRate on CROHME (67.4/68.4/65.4), which is a convincing cross-domain result for a generalist model.

The data collection pipeline is described in reasonable detail (sources, rendering with XeLaTeX, DPI variation, length-balanced sampling), and useful ablations are provided for training data composition (Table 2) and augmentation (Table 3), showing clear gains on CPE/SCE/HWE from the expanded data.
Public release of dataset and model supports reproducibility and follow-up work in a practically important, underserved task.
weaknesses: The main claimed technical contribution, the Length-Aware Module, is only weakly supported by its own ablation (Table 4): with LAM, BLEU is 0.917 vs 0.918 (SPE), 0.916 vs 0.893 (CPE), 0.616 vs 0.610 (SCE), 0.921 vs 0.920 (HWE). Only CPE improves, by ~2.3 BLEU, and some metrics are slightly worse with LAM. The text's claim that LAM 'significantly enhances the accuracy and stability' across varying complexities overstates this evidence.

Comparison fairness is a concern: UniMERNet is trained on ~1M samples including the full training splits of CROHME and HME100K, while Pix2tex and Texify are trained on much smaller data. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from the architecture versus sheer data scale, and this confound is not disentangled.

SCE ground-truth labels were produced with a commercial system (Mathpix) followed by manual correction and cross-verification by two annotators, but no annotation quality audit (e.g., inter-annotator agreement, error rate estimates) is reported; label noise or systematic Mathpix-style normalization could bias results in favor of UniMERNet, which is trained on similar data conventions.

The data ablation (Table 2) conflates quantity and diversity: Pix2tex, Pix2tex+HWE, and UniMER-1M differ in both size and content, so the specific benefit of 'length-aware sampling' versus simply more data cannot be isolated.

Writing quality needs improvement: repeated typos and inconsistencies ('senarios', 'ImageMagic', 'CHROME' for CROHME in Table 2 caption, 'stimulates the progress'), and the abstract/introduction promise more architectural novelty than Section 4 delivers (the method is essentially a Swin encoder + mBART decoder with a simple length-embedding head).

BLEU and edit distance are reported on UniMER-Test but ExpRate, arguably the most standard MER metric, is omitted there; no variance/significance analysis is provided for any result, and improvements such as +0.001-0.007 BLEU in Table 4 may be within run-to-run noise.

Recent LVLM baselines (Nougat, Vary) are discussed and shown qualitatively (Fig. 5) but are absent from the quantitative tables on UniMER-Test, leaving the comparison to LVLM-based document parsers incomplete.

strengths: The UniMER dataset is a genuine and useful resource contribution: UniMER-1M (1,061,791 LaTeX-image pairs) is roughly 7x larger than the previous largest open-source MER dataset, and the four-way UniMER-Test taxonomy (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) is a sensible decomposition of real-world deployment conditions that existing benchmarks (IM2LATEX, CROHME, HME100K, Pix2tex) do not cover.

The paper identifies and empirically demonstrates a real gap: Fig. 1 and Table 5 show that existing tools (Pix2tex, Texify) collapse on complex, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions (e.g., Pix2tex BLEU 0.092 on SCE, 0.012 on HWE), which motivates the benchmark.

Evaluation spans multiple standard metrics (BLEU, edit distance, ExpRate) and multiple established test sets (CROHME 2014/2016/2019, HME100K), including comparisons against dedicated handwritten-recognition systems, which is broader than many MER papers.

The reported headline results are strong: UniMERNet substantially outperforms Pix2tex and Texify on CPE/SCE (BLEU gains of ~0.226/0.196) and is competitive with or better than specialized HMER models on CROHME test sets.
Ablations on training-data composition (Table 2) are informative and show that the mixed UniMER-1M training data, rather than any single source, drives the cross-domain performance.
weaknesses: The headline architectural contribution, the Length-Aware Module, is not convincingly supported by the evidence. Table 4 shows LAM changes BLEU by at most +0.023 (CPE) and actually degrades SPE (0.918 to 0.917) and edit distance on SPE (0.056 to 0.058), while the text claims LAM 'significantly enhances the accuracy and stability.' A ~2% gain on one subset, with regressions elsewhere and no variance/significance analysis, does not justify the module being presented as a core contribution; it is unclear the module is better than noise.

The proposed method itself has limited novelty: Swin Transformer encoder + mBART decoder + standard image augmentations (dilation, erosion, weather noise) is a straightforward assembly of existing components (Donut-style architecture). The technical contribution rests almost entirely on the dataset and a weakly-validated module.

There is a potential circularity/contamination concern in the SCE test set: ground-truth labels were produced by running Mathpix (a commercial MER system) and then 'manually corrected.' If corrections were sparse, the benchmark partially measures similarity to Mathpix outputs, biasing comparisons; the paper does not report how many boxes required correction or inter-annotator agreement.

Possible test-set selection bias: the HWE test set uses only 3,000 of the 24,607 HME100K test images, with no explanation of how these were selected, which undermines comparability with prior HME100K results (e.g., CAN-ABM 68.1 ExpRate vs. UniMERNet 68.0 reported as 'comparable').

The comparison in Table 6 is not fully fair: UniMERNet is trained on a much larger, more diverse corpus (including the CROHME and HME100K training sets plus ~1M printed formulas) while baselines are trained on single datasets, yet the paper frames this as UniMERNet 'surpassing SOTA handwritten recognition models.' A data-matched or baseline-trained-on-mixed-data control is missing.

There are numerical inconsistencies that raise concerns about rigor: Table 3 reports an anomalous Pix2tex HWE edit distance of 0.004 without augmentation vs. 0.775 with augmentation (an implausible ~200x swing, likely an error); the text claims ExpRate gains of '1.5%, 5.3%, and 1.1%' over CROHME 2014/2016/2019, but Table 6 implies ~0.9% for 2019 (65.4 vs. 64.5); Fig. 1 numbers (e.g., SPE 87.3/90.6/91.7) do not match Table 5 (0.873/0.906/0.917 in format, but SCE 9.2 vs 0.092/HWE 34.1 vs 0.341 for Texify are inconsistent in scale).

The improvement attribution is muddled: Table 4 shows the model without LAM already achieves nearly all of the reported performance, meaning the gains mainly come from data scale and augmentation. The paper does not disentangle how much of the improvement over Pix2tex/Texify comes from training data volume (7x larger) versus the model design, e.g., by training a baseline architecture on UniMER-1M.

Some claims are overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'first study on MER towards complex real-world scenarios,' and typos/quality issues persist ('CHROME' for CROHME in Table 2 caption, 'senarios', 'CHOME 2019'), suggesting insufficient polish for a top-venue submission.

strengths: Substantial and genuinely useful dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (1,061,791 pairs) is ~6.7x larger than the largest prior open-source MER dataset, and UniMER-Test is thoughtfully decomposed into four realistic dimensions (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE), addressing a documented gap—existing benchmarks cover mainly simple printed or handwritten formulas.

The paper clearly demonstrates the motivation with strong empirical evidence: Fig. 1 and Tables 5 show that existing MER models (Pix2tex, Texify) and LVLMs (Nougat, Vary) degrade severely on screen-captured and long expressions (e.g., Pix2tex BLEU 0.092 on SCE), establishing the benchmark's value.

UniMERNet achieves meaningful, large improvements on the new benchmark (e.g., CPE BLEU 0.916 vs 0.690 for Texify) and is competitive with specialized handwritten-recognition SOTA on CROHME/HME100K (Table 6) despite being a general-purpose model—a convincing demonstration of transfer across formula types.

The data collection pipeline is described in reasonable detail (sources, LaTeX regularization, rendering, DPI variation, annotation and cross-verification of SCE), and the length-distribution analysis (Fig. 3) motivates the sampling strategy.
Resources are stated to be publicly available, which supports reproducibility and community impact; implementation details (GPUs, schedule, iterations, loss weights) are reported.
Ablations cover the three main components (training data, augmentation, LAM), and each is shown to contribute, e.g., augmentation improves SCE BLEU from 0.559 to 0.616.
weaknesses: The headline architectural contribution, the Length-Aware Module, is weakly supported by its own ablation. Table 4 shows mixed and marginal effects: with LAM, SPE BLEU drops (0.918→0.917), edit distance worsens on three of four subsets, and only CPE clearly improves (0.893→0.916). The claim that LAM 'significantly enhances the accuracy and stability' is overstated relative to this evidence, and no variance/significance analysis is provided to support such small deltas.

Potential train/test distribution overlap and leakage concerns are not addressed for the rendered subsets: CPE test data appears to be sampled from the same expanded/pipelined data used to build training data, and no deduplication or decontamination analysis against the Pix2tex-derived SPE test set is reported.

SCE ground truth is generated by a commercial model (Mathpix) followed by manual correction; inter-annotator agreement, correction rate, and label quality statistics are not reported. Evaluating models against labels produced by a recognition system risks biasing the benchmark, and this circularity deserves more scrutiny.

Comparisons with Pix2tex and Texify are confounded by training data scale: UniMERNet is trained on 1M samples (including CROHME/HME100K training data) while baselines use far smaller data, so gains cannot be attributed to the architecture; retraining baselines on UniMER-1M or adding a data-matched comparison would substantially strengthen the claims.

Architectural novelty is limited: the backbone (Swin encoder + mBART decoder, following Donut-style design) is standard, and LAM is a simple MLP/pooling module; the paper's strongest contribution is the dataset/benchmark rather than the method.

Metrics are incomplete and partly inconsistent: ExpRate is defined and used for CROHME/HME100K but not reported on UniMER-Test; Table 3 contains an apparent typo (Pix2tex+augment HWE EditDis 0.004 vs 0.775 without augment); BLEU/edit-distance on LaTeX strings are debatable proxies for mathematical correctness, and no evaluation of rendered validity or human judgment is provided.

Multiple presentation errors undermine polish: 'CHROME' for CROHME, 'CHOME 2019', 'senarios', the text reports four datasets but only three improvement percentages in the CROHME paragraph, and the LAM description is at times imprecise (e.g., 'mapped to the prediction space of symbol categories' vs. producing a length embedding).

No runtime/inference-efficiency comparison is given despite the claim that LAM enables efficient handling of long formulas, and the max-length interplay (1024 tokens vs formulas up to 7037 characters in Table 1) is not analyzed.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: UniMER-1M (~1.06M image-LaTeX pairs spanning simple/complex printed, screen-captured, and handwritten expressions) is considerably larger and more diverse than prior MER training sets (IM2LATEX-100K, Pix2tex), and the accompanying UniMER-Test benchmark (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE, ~23.8K samples) addresses a real gap in evaluating real-world robustness (Table 1, Fig. 2).

The dataset ablation (Table 2) is convincing and is the paper's strongest evidence: the same UniMERNet-B architecture trained on Pix2tex vs. Pix2tex&HWE vs. UniMER-1M shows large gains on CPE (BLEU 0.773→0.925, EditDis 0.194→0.056) and SCE (0.527→0.626), cleanly demonstrating that data scale/diversity—not just architecture—drives the improvement.

The fair-comparison experiment (Table 5, Texify* retrained on UniMER-1M) is commendable: it isolates the dataset contribution from the architectural contribution, showing Texify* already improves CPE from 0.690→0.900, with UniMERNet's modules adding further gains.

Thorough ablation coverage: architecture modules (Table 3), pre-training (Table 6), data augmentation (Table 7), and encoder/decoder depth (Tables 8-9) are all examined, and appendix details (rendering settings, normalization, deduplication via perceptual hashing, augmentation pipeline) support reproducibility. Code, data, and models are stated to be released.

Consistent speed-accuracy analysis: the Squeeze Attention module is well motivated (decoder autoregression as the throughput bottleneck) and delivers a measured ~23% FPS improvement with minimal accuracy loss.
Qualitative analysis (Fig. 5) is appropriately cautious, e.g., adapting Nougat's input format for isolated-formula comparison rather than dismissing its failures.
weaknesses: The architectural contribution is incremental: FGE (overlapping conv patch embedding), CE (depthwise conv before attention/MLP), RSW, and SA are well-known techniques (conv-attention hybrids, ResNet bottlenecks) applied to the Swin+mBART recipe already used by Donut/Texify/Nougat. Per-module gains are small (Table 3: FGE+CE adds ~2 BLEU points on SCE; most rows differ by <0.01), and the headline gains are attributable primarily to the dataset rather than the network.

Potential train/test circularity undermines parts of the benchmark: CPE train and test are 'randomly selected' from the same expanded Arxiv/Wikipedia pool (risking near-duplicate leakage across splits), and SCE ground truth is produced by Mathpix—the same commercial system family used by the authors' organization—then manually corrected; the extent of correction and inter-annotator agreement is not quantified, so SCE labels may embed Mathpix's own biases.

ExpRate is defined as a metric but appears absent from the main comparison tables (Tables 2, 5, 7 report only BLEU/Edit Distance), and the paper does not evaluate on the standard CROHME test sets with ExpRate as is customary in HMER literature, making it impossible to position the method against specialized HMER state-of-the-art (CAN, CoMER, etc.). The HWE BLEU of 0.895 cannot be contextualized.

Evaluation is confined to the authors' own benchmark; there are no experiments on IM2LATEX-100K's original test split or other external test sets, which weakens generality claims beyond the self-defined distribution.

Internal inconsistencies and overclaims reduce polish: UniMER-Test size is stated as 23,789 in the text but 23,757 in Table 1; Table 2's caption says 'HME' while the text/table header says HWE; the claim of being 'the first study on MER targeting complex real-world scenarios' overstates novelty given prior noisy/real-world HME100K work; the Introduction text appears cut off mid-sentence ('All data, models, and code are available at').

No statistical significance, variance across seeds, or error analysis by formula length is provided; with BLEU differences as small as 0.003-0.009 between UniMERNet variants and Texify* (e.g., 0.906→0.909 on SPE), the reported superiority on SPE is not demonstrably meaningful.

Comparison baselines are limited to Pix2tex, Texify, and Nougat; recent specialized MER models and general VLM-based extraction systems are discussed in related work but not quantitatively compared, so 'new benchmark in open-source MER' is supported only against a narrow baseline set.

strengths: The UniMER dataset (UniMER-1M training set with ~1M image-LaTeX pairs and the UniMER-Test benchmark covering SPE, CPE, SCE, and HWE) addresses a genuine gap: existing MER benchmarks focus on clean, simple printed or handwritten formulas, and the demonstrated performance collapse of prior methods on complex and screen-captured expressions (Figure 1, Table 5) motivates the work well.

The paper is generally transparent about confounds: the Texify* baseline retrained on UniMER-1M isolates the dataset contribution from the architecture contribution (Table 5), and the ablations in Tables 2, 3, 6, 7 separately quantify training data, augmentation, pre-training, and architectural modules.

Extensive supporting material (appendix with sampling procedure, deduplication, LaTeX normalization, augmentation ablations, and encoder/decoder depth studies) improves reproducibility and shows the dataset construction was done with reasonable care.

Releasing data, models, and code, plus a lightweight variant (UniMERNet-T) that is both faster and more accurate than Texify, gives the work practical utility for the document-understanding community.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: UniMERNet is a Swin-Transformer encoder + mBART decoder (the Donut/Nougat/Texify recipe) with incremental modifications. Fine-grained overlapping patch embedding, depthwise-conv enhancement, and attention bottlenecking are all well-established techniques, and the ablation gains are small (Table 3: BLEU improvements of ~0.9-2.2%, and FGE alone changes SPE from 0.903 to 0.903 and SCE from 0.579 to 0.584). The paper's real contribution is the dataset, and the architecture section reads as engineering rather than a substantive methodological advance.

The evaluation protocol has a fundamental fairness problem: UniMER-Test is constructed largely from the same distribution as UniMER-1M (rendered Arxiv/Wikipedia formulas for SPE/CPE, and even the SCE annotations were produced with Mathpix, a system whose pipeline is closely related to the authors'), so the reported SOTA results partially measure distribution match rather than universal generalization. There is no held-out evaluation on independent benchmarks (e.g., zero-shot evaluation on original IM2LATEX or CROHME test splits) to substantiate the 'universal' claim.

The SCE subset is small and of questionable quality: only 4,744 samples labeled by two annotators and recognized via Mathpix with manual correction; potential circularity and annotation bias are not analyzed. No inter-annotator agreement or error analysis on this subset is provided.

Some claims are under-supported. The Squeeze Attention module is motivated only by a throughput argument and shows near-zero accuracy change (Table 3: 0.894 vs 0.897 CPE, 0.893 vs 0.893 HWE); its information-loss behavior is not characterized. The RSW (Remove Shift Window) justification is qualitative ('receptive field is already enlarged') without receptive-field measurement. Pre-training uses '16 million in-house image-text pairs' (Table 6) that are not released, weakening reproducibility of that ablation.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: Table 1 lists UniMER test size as 23,757 while the text says 23,789; Table 2's caption refers to 'HME' vs 'CHROME' (misspelling of CROHME) inconsistently with the HWE label elsewhere; the improvement of UniMERNet-B over Texify on HWE is described as an 'absolute improvement of 0.554' which is actually 0.895 vs 0.341 from the original Texify (a comparison inflated by Texify's lack of handwriting training data); the writing contains typos ('designe', 'piratical').

Missing standard baselines and comparisons: no comparison with specialized HMER methods (CAN, CoMER, SAN) on the HWE subset even though those datasets are included, and no comparison against recent LVLM-based approaches beyond a qualitative note, despite the introduction framing these as competitors. ExpRate, the standard HMER metric the authors list, is never actually reported in any table.

BLEU on its own is a weak metric for LaTeX generation (syntactically invalid output can score well); the paper mentions Edit Distance but does not report validity rates or render-and-compare evaluation, which would be more meaningful for the practical use case emphasized.

strengths: The dataset contribution is substantial and well-motivated: UniMER-1M (~1.06M image-LaTeX pairs) is roughly 5x larger than prior MER training sets (Table 1), and the four-part UniMER-Test (SPE/CPE/SCE/HWE) explicitly targets realistic deployment scenarios (long formulas, screen captures, handwriting) that existing benchmarks like IM2LATEX and CROHME do not cover.

The dataset construction is documented in useful detail: LaTeX normalization rules, XeLaTeX rendering settings with multiple fonts and DPIs (appendix Listing 1), length-balanced resampling of CPE (Figure 6), and perceptual-hash image deduplication for SCE are all specified, supporting reproducibility.

Experimental evidence is unusually thorough for this area. The paper cleanly disentangles data effects from architecture effects: Table 5 shows Texify* (same architecture, trained on UniMER-1M) already improves CPE BLEU from 0.690 to 0.900, and Table 2/7 show further gains from the full dataset plus augmentation. This honest attribution strengthens the central claim that data scale/diversity is the dominant factor.

Ablations cover each proposed module (FGE, CE, RSW, SA in Table 3), pre-training with 16M text-image pairs (Table 6), encoder/decoder depth (Tables 8-9), and qualitative comparisons (Figure 5). Model sizes and FPS are reported, and the lightweight UniMERNet-T Pareto point (7.20 img/s, 1.73x faster than Texify) is practically relevant.

The paper is transparent that the architecture alone provides modest gains (BLEU improvements of 0.9-2.2% in Table 3), which is a scientifically honest framing even if it tempers the 'novel architecture' contribution.
Models, data, and code are stated to be publicly released, and the benchmark fills a genuine gap in MER evaluation.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited. FGE (overlapping 3x3 convolutions for patch embedding), CE (depthwise conv before attention/MLP), RSW (removing shifted windows), and SA (low-rank query/key projection) are all individually well-known modifications; the paper does not clearly articulate what is new versus standard practice, and per-module gains in Table 3 are small (e.g., FGE+CE improve SCE BLEU from 0.579 to 0.599).

The SCE labels were produced by Mathpix and then 'manually corrected' by two annotators. The exact annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement, correction rate, and residual label-noise level are unreported. Since SCE is where the headline gains are claimed, label quality on this subset is a material validity concern.

Potential train/test contamination: both UniMER-1M training data and test sources are drawn from Arxiv/Wikipedia/StackExchange, and the deduplication strategy described applies only to the SCE test set. No dedup between rendered training formulas and CPE/SPE test formulas is reported, so the large CPE gain could partly reflect memorization.

ExpRate is introduced as an evaluation metric (and is the standard metric for CROHME), but no ExpRate results are reported anywhere. Comparisons with dedicated HMER methods (CAN, CoMER, syntax-aware networks) on CROHME/HME100K are also absent, so superiority on handwritten expressions relative to the HMER literature is not established; the HWE improvement over Texify* is only +0.007 BLEU.

BLEU as the primary metric is acknowledged in the appendix to be affected by LaTeX ambiguity, yet the evaluation relies almost entirely on BLEU and Edit Distance. Normalization is claimed to mitigate this, but no analysis of metric sensitivity (e.g., ExpRate or rendered-image fidelity) is provided.

All results appear to be single runs without variance, significance testing, or multiple seeds, despite several claimed improvements being on the order of 0.1-0.9 BLEU (e.g., SPE gains of UniMERNet-B over Texify* are 0.009 BLEU with EditDis 0.060 vs 0.067).

The 16M pre-training pairs (Table 6) are described as 'in-house' and their release status is unclear, weakening reproducibility of the pre-trained results; similarly, licensing and per-source breakdowns of UniMER-1M are thin.

Minor presentation issues: text refers to 'HME' vs 'HWE' and 'CHROME' vs 'CROHME' inconsistently (Table 2 caption), some editing errors ('real piratical use', 'designe'), and the claimed SA speedup (24%) coexists with 'slightly reduced precision' that is not quantified separately in Table 5 configurations.
